text: Methods §1: A two-arm trial compares intervention A and usual care on the prespecified primary outcome. The manuscript calls the allocation randomized but explicitly states that the sequence-generation and allocation-concealment procedures are not described in the manuscript or supplied supplement. Results §2: The central efficacy claim relies on this randomized comparison. The excerpt provides no evidence establishing how allocation was actually conducted.

Methods §2: Six donors each supplied three technical wells in vehicle and three in treatment. We averaged technical wells within each donor/condition, then analyzed the six paired donor differences, treating donors as independent units. Results §3: The estimated difference is +2 units with a reported 95% interval of −3 to +7. Discussion §4: This estimate is imprecise and does not establish a direction; inference is restricted to the donor-derived system studied. No independent-well test was used.

Methods §1: In a cross-sectional survey, adults self-selected whether to use supplement S. Current use and current symptoms were measured at the same visit. The reported comparison is unadjusted; users and nonusers differ in baseline health behaviors. Results §2: Users reported fewer symptoms. Discussion §3: These results prove that taking S prevents the development of symptoms.

Methods §3: A classifier uses multiple images per patient. We split patients into training, validation, and test groups before preprocessing or fitting; no patient contributes to more than one group. Preprocessing is fitted on training data, tuning uses validation data, and the test group is untouched until final evaluation. Results §4: Reported AUC is 0.94 on new patients from the same hospital. Discussion §5: No cross-hospital or deployment-readiness claim is made; other settings require further validation.

Results §2: A two-sided superiority test estimates a difference of +4 units, with a reported 95% interval from −4 to +12 and p = 0.32. Differences of 3 units in either direction would be scientifically important. Discussion §3: Because p exceeds 0.05, the intervention has no scientifically meaningful effect and the groups are equivalent. Methods §1: No equivalence margin or equivalence analysis was prespecified or performed.

Methods §2: This codebook-based content analysis prespecifies that coding reliability will be considered adequate only if Cohen's kappa is at least 0.80. The central claim is that the final categories were reproducibly coded according to that criterion. Results §3: Final double-coded material yielded kappa = 0.84, and no further reconciliation or reliability assessment was performed. The text concludes that the prespecified reliability threshold was met.

Methods §2: Six donors each supplied three technical wells in vehicle and three in treatment. All 18 wells per condition were treated as independent observations in an unpaired test; donor membership was not included in the analysis. Results §3: This well-level test was the sole uncertainty analysis. Discussion §4: Its statistical significance establishes a treatment increase in the donor-derived system. Donor identifiers and raw measurements remain available for reanalysis.

Methods §1: In a cross-sectional survey, adults self-selected whether to use supplement S. Current use and symptoms were measured at the same visit. The comparison is unadjusted; users and nonusers differ in baseline health behaviors. Results §2: Users reported fewer symptoms. Discussion §3: This is an unadjusted association. Confounding, selection, reverse causation, and absent temporal ordering prevent a conclusion that S prevents symptoms. Findings are exploratory and restricted to this sample.

Methods §2: This codebook-based content analysis prespecifies that coding reliability will be considered adequate only if Cohen's kappa is at least 0.80. The central claim is that the final categories were reproducibly coded according to that criterion. Results §3: Final double-coded material yielded kappa = 0.42, and no further reconciliation or reliability assessment was performed. The text concludes that the prespecified reliability threshold was met.

Methods §1: A two-arm trial compares intervention A and usual care on the prespecified primary outcome. A statistician generated the random sequence with computer software. An independent centralized allocation service concealed assignments from recruiting staff until enrollment was complete for each participant. Results §2: The central efficacy claim relies on this randomized comparison. This excerpt makes no claim about masking or other trial procedures.

Methods §3: A classifier uses multiple images per patient. Images were randomly split so that every patient's images appear in both training and test sets. The test set therefore contains images of patients whose other images were used for fitting. Results §4: Reported AUC is 0.94. Discussion §5: This evaluation establishes performance on entirely new patients who contributed no data to training. No patient-disjoint evaluation is reported.

Results §2: A two-sided superiority test estimates a difference of +4 units, with a reported 95% interval from −4 to +12 and p = 0.32. Differences of 3 units in either direction would be scientifically important. Discussion §3: The estimate is inconclusive and compatible with important effects in either direction. Nonsignificance does not establish equivalence or absence of a meaningful effect. Methods §1: No equivalence margin or equivalence analysis was prespecified or performed.
